lesson.title: Lock down your phone
lesson.subtitle: Six settings that protect everything on it

video.title: Lock down your phone
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Staff room at break. Joseph sits at his desk; three colleagues queue with phones held out. Above them, three small thought bubbles: a keypad showing 1234, a game icon reaching for a message bubble, an empty bus seat. Joseph rubs his forehead and smiles.
scenes.animation: Thought bubbles pop one by one, 300 ms apart. Small push-in on Joseph.
scenes.narration: Three phones, one break time. A lock code of one-two-three-four, a game that wants to read messages, and a phone left on a bus — with no backup. Right. Let’s fix this.
scenes.sound: Staff room chatter; light music bed starts.
scenes.vids: Character: illustrated computer studies teacher, ink outlines. Show the keypad digits large and simple; no phone brand shapes or logos.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the lesson title and the cyber track chip with its icon.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: six quick settings that lock down your phone — and everything on it.
scenes.vids: Use the Darsi title template (see brand kit). Keep the chip as icon + word.

scenes.visual: A phone opens like a cabinet to show what’s inside: an envelope, a mobile money wallet, a photo, a contacts book. The doors close and a padlock clicks shut. A keypad shows 1234 and a birthday cake, both fading to grey, replaced by six blank dots.
scenes.animation: Cabinet doors swing open, then shut; padlock click. Grey fade on the weak codes, 200 ms.
scenes.narration: Your phone holds your email, mobile money, photos and parents’ numbers. If someone gets in, they get all of that. So start with the screen lock. Codes like one-two-three-four or your birth year are guessed first. Choose six digits or more, with no link to you.
scenes.sound: Cabinet creak; a firm padlock click.
scenes.vids: Show the new PIN only as dots. Never show a real person’s code.

scenes.visual: A house with an open window; a small download arrow flies in and the window closes. Then a shop-bag icon with a shield (the official store) stands next to a chat bubble holding a file, which gets a gentle cross.
scenes.animation: The window shuts with a soft thud as the arrow lands. A cross draws over the chat file in 300 ms.
scenes.narration: Next, updates. Many fix security holes criminals could use — so don’t keep tapping “later”. Low on data? Update on Wi-Fi or with a bundle. And install apps only from your phone’s official store — never from a file or link in a chat.
scenes.sound: Soft thud of the window; a light click.
scenes.vids: Use a generic shop-bag icon for the store; never show a real store logo.

scenes.visual: Clean card with the cyber track chip. An app tile in the middle; around it, five permission icons light up one by one: camera, microphone, contacts book, map pin, message bubble. A question mark hovers over the tile.
scenes.animation: Icons light up 250 ms apart; the question mark bobs once.
scenes.narration: Then check app permissions — what each app is allowed to use: camera, microphone, contacts, location, messages. Ask one question: does this app need that to do its job?
scenes.vids: Keep the card on screen for at least 6 seconds so teachers can read it in a second language.

scenes.visual: Split screen. Left: a map app tile linked to a location pin, with a blue check. Right: a torch app tile reaching for a contacts book, with a cross. A thumb flips the torch’s permission switch to off.
scenes.animation: Check and cross pop 200 ms apart; the switch slides to off.
scenes.narration: A map needs your location. A torch app doesn’t need your contacts. If the answer is no, switch the permission off — or delete the app.
scenes.vids: Use flat generic app tiles; no real app icons. Blue for the check, never green.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor bursts in, delighted, holding up his phone: a new torch app asks to read his messages. Two answer cards drop in: a check (allow it) and a switch turned off (say no).
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! My new torch app wants to read my messages. That’s fine, isn’t it?
scenes.sound: Two gentle ‘pop’ sounds for the cards.
scenes.vids: The app pauses here (diamond marker). For the MP4 shared outside the app, hold this frame for 3 seconds with a small countdown ring.

scenes.visual: The ‘say no’ card gets a blue check badge. The message permission switch slides off, and the torch still shines.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms). Quick 0.8 s confetti of three shapes in kola, sunbird and ink.
scenes.narration: No. A torch doesn’t need your messages. Switch that permission off, or delete the app and use the phone’s own torch.
scenes.vids: Use blue for correct (never green) and always pair it with the check icon.

scenes.visual: A busy bus stop. A phone slips from a bag onto a seat and the bus drives off. Joseph, on another phone, opens a map: a pin pulses on the bus route. He taps ring, then lock.
scenes.animation: The bus slides off-screen; the map pin pulses twice; a lock icon pops onto the lost phone.
scenes.narration: Now get ready for a lost phone. Check that “find my device” is on today — you can’t switch it on once the phone is gone. Then, from another phone, you can ring it, lock it or erase it.
scenes.sound: Bus engine fades; a phone ring tone.
scenes.vids: Generic map with no place names or brand marks. Draw the bus as a simple flat shape.

scenes.visual: Photos, a contacts book and lesson notes float up from a phone into a cloud shape and onto a laptop. The phone breaks into pieces; a new phone appears and everything floats back into it.
scenes.animation: Items float up in an arc over 1.5 s; the new phone fills back up in reverse.
scenes.narration: And back up your photos and contacts — to your online account or a computer. Low on data? Let backups run on Wi-Fi only. Then a lost phone is a bad day, not a disaster.
scenes.sound: Gentle whoosh up, then back down.
scenes.vids: Use a generic cloud shape, not a brand. Keep the broken phone cartoonish, not dramatic.

scenes.visual: Joseph turns to the viewer holding a colleague’s phone with a keypad and a small cake icon on screen. Three answer cards bounce in: keep it, change to six digits with no link to her, turn the lock off.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A colleague’s lock code is her birth year. What’s the best advice?
scenes.vids: Second diamond marker — the app pauses for the question. In the MP4, hold for 3 seconds, then highlight ‘six digits with no link to her’.

scenes.visual: The six-digits card gets the check badge. Then the phone check-up appears: five icons in a circle around a phone — padlock, download arrow, shield, map pin, stacked discs.
scenes.animation: Icons travel round the circle and settle, 250 ms apart.
scenes.on_screen_text: Lock · Update · Apps · Find · Back up
scenes.narration: Six digits with no link to her. Remember the check-up: a strong lock, updates, apps from the official store, sensible permissions, find my device, and a backup.
scenes.vids: Hold the check-up circle for 5 seconds.

scenes.visual: Joseph’s classroom. A big phone is drawn on the board with six icons around it. Pairs of pupils role-play: one holds a paper phone and a problem card, the other points to an icon on the board and explains. End card: Darsi mark and ‘Next: Safer school groups’.
scenes.animation: Pupils point; icons on the board light up as they are chosen. End card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: draw a big phone on the board. In pairs, pupils role-play a phone clinic — one brings a problem card, the other picks the fix and explains why.
scenes.sound: Music resolves; no end jingle longer than 1 s.
scenes.vids: Classroom: illustrated pupils in local school uniforms; avoid stereotyped imagery. End card from the Darsi template; no app names on screen.

checkpoints.prompt: A new torch app wants to read your messages. Should you allow it?

options.text: Yes — apps need lots of access
No — switch it off or delete the app

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a torch only needs to switch on the light. Reading messages has nothing to do with its job.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a torch doesn’t need your messages. Switch that permission off, or delete the app.

checkpoints.prompt: A colleague’s lock code is her birth year. What’s the best advice?

options.text: Keep it — it’s easy to remember
Change it to six digits with no link to her
Turn the lock off to save time

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a birth year is easy to guess. Six digits with no link to her is much harder.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a birth year is guessed early, and no lock is worse. Six digits with no link to her is safer.

video.vids_prompt: Create a 3 minute animated explainer video for teachers titled “Lock down your phone”. Style: flat, friendly illustration with bold ink outlines, light grey backgrounds, a tangerine (#ff6a2b) brand colour and hibiscus pink (#f04a7e); no gradients or blur. Main character: Mr Joseph Mwangi, a computer studies teacher. Follow the script scene by scene: three colleagues with phone problems; a strong screen lock; updates and the official app store; checking app permissions; a torch app that wants messages; find my device for a lost phone; backups; two quiz pauses; end with a phone clinic role-play. Use the narration exactly as written, a warm, calm voice, and keep on-screen text to six words or fewer per scene. No logos or brand names on screen.
